Fine-grained structured pruning of reasoning LLMs is typically followed by 
recovery training. RLVR is widely believed superior to SFT for this purpose. 
We challenge this assumption: on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, we show that 
the pruning criterion—not the recovery paradigm—determines post-pruning 
reasoning quality at moderate sparsity. When pruning preserves representational 
diversity, SFT and GRPO produce near-identical accuracy despite divergent 
reward trajectories, a phenomenon we term reward-accuracy decoupling. We 
propose RASP, a scoring function that combines gradient importance with 
CKA-based diversity, and identify a recovery capacity spectrum where 
diversity-preserving criteria sustain RL exploration while importance-dominated 
criteria lead to reward collapse. Our findings hold across multiple benchmarks 
and show preliminary cross-scale evidence.

Fine-grained structured pruning of reasoning Large Language Models (LLMs), which removes MLP channel groups rather than entire layers, is typically followed by recovery training via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) or Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR).
RLVR is widely assumed to be the superior recovery paradigm, yet our results suggest this advantage is attributable to the pruning criterion rather than an inherent property of RL\@.
We propose Recovery-Aware Structured Pruning (\rasp{}), a parameterized scoring function that combines gradient importance with CKA-based representational diversity.
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, we identify a \emph{recovery capacity spectrum}: under GRPO training, diversity-preserving criteria sustain active learning while importance-dominated criteria exhibit reward collapse.
Despite this divergence in training dynamics, SFT and GRPO yield near-identical downstream accuracy at 20--25\% MLP sparsity---a phenomenon we term \emph{reward-accuracy decoupling}.
These findings hold across GSM8K, MATH-500, and MBPP, with preliminary cross-scale and cross-model evidence on Qwen2.5-family models.
